20922-the-young-treasure-hunter-or-fred-:
Rich strikes near Cartersville draw boys to drive ore carts in The Young Treasure Hunter. Fred Stanley hears of a new camp called New Strike and keenly wants a place. Frank V. Webster sets his 1909 tale on that lure of gold.

Alaska's cold, mines, and rough camps test Fred and his friends at each step. Webster wrote brisk tales of boys who earn their way by grit. Treasure, work, and peril mix in the classic series mould. Readers get a clear slice of gold-rush fever as it was sold to boys, full of hope, hazard, and hard lessons.
22409-a-woman-who-went-to-alaska:
A Woman Who Went to Alaska, dated 1902, records a gold-rush journey north. Its picture captions map the route in telling snapshots. Porcupine Canyon and White Pass appear among the first views.

Other captions show Dawson reached in winter and Eagle City on the Yukon. The Yukon steamer Hannah carries travelers in one image. Fellow travelers pose in another photograph along the way. Claim Number Nine on Anvil Creek shows the goal. Nome's Bonanza Creek claims complete the mining picture. The Skagway River, seen from the train, marks the road home. A woman's own account of that rush still makes fresh reading.
22871-over-the-rocky-mountains-to-alaska:
Notre Dame's campus glows at the start of Over the Rocky Mountains to Alaska, dated 1899. Lawns, winding forest ways, and the blasts of the University Band fill the last day of the school year with joy. The scene feels like an elysium in summer, the narrator says, and memorable forever.

From that gentle farewell the book turns north and west. The journey crosses the Rockies toward Alaska in the gold-rush years, when the territory drew crowds of hopeful travelers. Readers get scenery, hardship, and the peculiar mix of students, miners, and sightseers on the trail. Travel narratives of the period sold wonder by the page. This one begins in Indiana shade and ends under northern skies.
2494-for-greater-things-the-story-of-sai:
William T. Kane tells the story of Saint Stanislaus Kostka, the young Polish Jesuit who ran away from home to follow his calling and died at eighteen. For Greater Things follows Stanislaus from his noble family through his flight to Rome, his novitiate, and his early death, with devotion and idealism at its center. Kane writes for young Catholic readers.

The biography's tone is reverent and inspiring, presenting its hero as a model of youthful faith. Readers interested in saints' lives will find a clear, earnest account. It serves as an introduction to a beloved Jesuit saint.
28724-in-the-high-valley-being-the-fifth:
Susan Coolidge wrote this 1891 novel, the fifth and last volume of the Katy Did series. It opens on the north Devon coast in late May, at Copplestone Grange, an old red-brick house from the sixteenth century. It then follows its characters across the Atlantic to a high valley in America. Chapters move from Miss Opdyke from New York to thorns and roses, an unconditional surrender, and a double knot.

The book closes the story of Katy Carr and her circle, carrying them from English scenes to a new home in the mountains. Coolidge's readers, who had followed Katy from childhood illness to school and marriage, get a satisfying farewell. It is a gentle, well-written family novel, and a fitting end to one of America's best-loved girls' series.
29113-the-trail-of-a-sourdough-life-in-a:
May Kellogg Sullivan published this Alaska memoir with the Gorham Press in Boston in 1910. Sullivan defines her title term at the start. A sourdough is a miner who has wintered once in Alaska and watched the ice break up. She herself made seven trips over ten years.

Chapters cover the miner's reasons, life under the tundra, a hidden ledge, and a new Klondike. Sullivan writes from firsthand travel in the North, about flour without baking powder, dough kept from batch to batch, and camps beyond civilization. Readers get a woman pioneer's Alaska, practical and observant, from the gold-rush years.
29242-made-in-tanganyika:
Carl Jacobi wrote this science fiction story about Martin Sutter, who turns forty and decides life is too short for the rut of twenty years. Sutter empties his account at the Explosion City Third Federal Bank and buys an electric runabout with a blue bonnet, retailing for three thousand credits. He takes Highway 56 for a driving lesson in his new ground-car.

Jacobi's magazine introduction warns readers to be cautious the next time they turn on a television set, especially one made in Tanganyika. Sutter's fresh start soon meets a necromantic nightmare. Readers get a witty, unsettling tale where a midlife purchase and a household machine open the door to something strange.
30812-with-the-french-in-france-and-salo:
Richard Harding Davis, author of With the Allies, wrote this illustrated book on the French in France and Salonika, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in April 1916. Davis was one of America's best known war correspondents, and this volume reports from the Western Front and from the Allied front at Salonika in the First World War. Its title joins two fronts that most American readers knew only from headlines.

The book follows French soldiers, officers, and civilians, with Davis's eye for camp, trench, and town life. It captures the mood of France in wartime and the strange, far-flung campaign in the Balkans, where Allies held a line far from home. Historians and general readers will find vivid, first-hand reporting from a journalist who made the war feel close and human.
30898-a-new-bog-lemming-genus-synaptomys:
J. Knox Jones Jr. wrote this short scientific paper for the University of Kansas Publications, Museum of Natural History, volume nine, number thirteen, pages 385 to 388, dated May 12, 1958. In autumn 1952 Jones obtained a southern bog lemming, Synaptomys cooperi, at Rock Creek State Fish Hatchery in Dundy County, in extreme southwestern Nebraska. That site was the westernmost record for the species in North America.

Jones first reported that specimen in 1954, provisionally as Synaptomys cooperi gossii, the subspecies of eastern Nebraska. In late November 1956, J. R. Alcorn collected three more bog lemmings at the same hatchery, and Jones found that this relict population differed from gossii and from all other subspecies. He therefore names it Synaptomys cooperi relictus, with an adult female skin and skull as its type. It is a concise paper for mammal students.
31804-francezka:
Molly Elliot Seawell's 1902 novel Francezka is narrated by a devoted servant of Maurice, Count of Saxe, marshal-general of France. The narrator maintains his master is the greatest, bravest, finest, and handsomest man who ever lived, and says his sword is the invincible argument against anyone who disputes it.

Chapters move from the heart of Paris and a little actress to a rescue, a balcony, a crimson mantle, a lost cause, and an impatient lover. Readers get a historical romance of eighteenth-century France, told by a loyal retainer whose praise of his master is half the entertainment.
32159-mammals-from-southeastern-alaska:
Rollin H. Baker and James S. Findley's paper on mammals from southeastern Alaska appeared in the University of Kansas Publications, Museum of Natural History, volume 7, number 5, pages 473 to 477, published April 21, 1954. The paper reports a sizable collection of mammals received by the museum from J. R. Alcorn and Albert A. Alcorn, taken in Alaska in the summer of 1951.

The Alcorns revisited localities where they had collected in 1947 and 1948, and added specimens from places not previously visited near Anchorage and Haines. They also collected on Sullivan Island, a small wooded island in Lynn Canal. Part of the funds for field work came from outside support, as the paper notes. Readers get a short faunal report, useful for the distribution of Alaskan mammals rather than for general natural history.
37101-humpback-whales-in-glacier-bay-nat:
Humpback Whales in Glacier Bay National Monument, Alaska, is a federal report. The Marine Mammal Commission issued it in February 1980 at Washington as report MMC-79/01. The Commerce Department technical information service distributed it, availability unlimited, it notes. Portions of the best copy furnished were illegible, the release notice owns plainly.

A report documentation page gives the October 1979 report date and numbers. The commission office sat at 1625 I Street in Washington at that time. Glacier Bay whales, their numbers and habits, are the report subject in full. Federal marine mammal oversight produced this study for public release in print. Researchers and park managers are its plain intended readers.
43058-marie-tarnowska:
Vivanti Chartres wrote this life of Marie Tarnowska, a Russian countess whose name filled the papers of her day. Marie Nicolaevna Tarnowska fronts the book in a plate. Her tale is one of love, wealth, and a famed trial for murder.

Tarnowska's beauty and her wild life in Russia and abroad drew all eyes in the years before the Great War. A lover's death and a court case in Venice made her a byword across Europe. Vivanti writes as a near hand, with warmth for her subject. Readers of 1915 got the woman behind the headlines: her charm, her falls, and the men ruined in her train, in a life that reads like a novel.
43284-wilderness-a-journal-of-quiet-adve:
Rockwell Kent, artist and writer, kept a journal of a stay in Alaska that he calls Wilderness. The book came out in New York and London in 1920, with drawings by Kent himself. Dorothy Canfield adds a short first word. Kent gives the book to old Olson and to his young son of Fox Island.

Kent writes as a man glad to live rough and plain. The heads run from first sight and landing to chores and deep winter. Fox Island is home base for work, cold, and calm days. Readers who love the far north get a quiet, close diary of one hard, bright season.
43374-gulf-and-glacier-or-the-percivals-:
Gulf and Glacier sends the Percival family north to Alaska. Willis Boyd Allen wrote the tale for his Pine Cone Stories set. Lothrop of Boston put out the book with a copyright of 1892. The set holds six cloth volumes sold at one dollar each. Pine Cones, Kelp, and Cloud and Cliff stand in that same set.

Chapter one starts the clan at a Boston rail depot in July. Forest, prairie, and a home letter mark the long cross-country ride. A glacier and a bear share a chapter in the wild north. Victoria, Sitka, and the Muir Glacier pass in the tour of sights. A silver-tip bear and a king's daughter lost in a freight car appear. Wonderland and white lilies close the trip before the home run.
44077-adventures-in-alaska:
Adventures in Alaska is a book of travels by Samuel Hall Young, printed by Fleming Revell in 1919. Young also wrote Alaska Days with John Muir and The Klondike Clan. The front pages carry praise from the New York Times and The Nation for the earlier book.

Eight chapters tell of Young's own Alaskan years. The last tales are Nina and the Bears and The Absurd Walrus. A frontispiece shows Young stalking walrus in an oomiak, the trip on which he got the ivory for his gavels. Reviewers called the book a breezy outdoor tale, full of the wild beauties of the Alaskan wilds. It is also a living portrait of Muir at the great moments of his career, drawn by the friend who travelled at his side.
44688-to-and-through-nebraska:
To and Through Nebraska is a travel book by Frances Fulton, who signs herself a Pennsylvania girl. It was printed at Lincoln, Nebraska, by the state printers in 1884. The book claims no merit but truth, she says, and is offered to the friends who made the long travel pleasant.

A word to the reader maps the chapters. The first tells of the Nebraska Mutual Aid Colony from Bradford, Pennsylvania, and its settling in the north-west of the state. Their trials and triumphs stand beside the Elkhorn, Niobrara, and Keya Paha rivers. Later chapters take up the Platte valley, the Big Blue, and the Republican. The state's history, climate, schools, and liquor laws get a chapter of their own. Fulton rode the three great railroads of the state, for nearly nine hundred miles in all.
46468-a-voyage-round-the-world-from-1806:
Archibald Campbell, a Scots sailor, told of his six years' voyage round the world in this book. Duke and Browne printed this third American edition at Charleston in 1822. A chart of the Eclipse's long boat, from Sannack to Kodiak in 1807, heads it.

Japan, Kamchatka, the Aleutian Islands, and the Sandwich Islands stand in his title's roll. Shipwreck is its dark heart: Campbell was wrecked on Sannack, then wrecked again in the ship's long boat. He came home by way of years among the Russians of Alaska. A state of the Sandwich Islands and a word list of their tongue close the tale. Sailors bought such books by the chestful.
48550-campaigning-in-kaffirland-or-scene:
Campaigning in Kaffirland is Captain King's account of scenes and adventures in the Kaffir War of 1851 and 1852. King served with the 74th Highlanders in South Africa. The book was published in London in 1853 with illustrations. Its preface disowns any aim at a full history of the war.

King wrote the pages in leisure hours in a lonely fort or by the camp fire after the day's fatigue. They follow the movements of one division, often of a single brigade. The first chapters tell of the voyage out and the state of the country on arrival. His aim, he says, is to give a general idea of the land and of the passing events of the campaign.
49315-ourika:
Claire de Duras wrote this short French novel, printed in London in English in 1824. A line from Byron stands at the front: to be alone, this is solitude. The narrator, a young physician lately come from Montpellier to Paris, is called one morning to a sick nun.

The convent stands in the Faubourg St. Jacques, lately re-established after Napoleon's permission. Part of the building was destroyed in the Revolution, and its cloister lies open on one side. The paving stones of that cloister are tombs, their inscriptions half worn away. There the doctor meets Ourika, whose sad story he tells.
50752-anthropological-survey-in-alaska:
Ales Hrdlicka's Anthropological Survey in Alaska reads as a field report on the native peoples of the far north. The contents map a long trip: Juneau and the coast Indians first, then up the Yukon past Tanana, Ruby, Galena, Nulato, and Kaltag. Nome, Barrow, and the island of St Michael close the route.

Each stop yields notes on villages, old sites, and present life, with finds such as pottery and the grooved stone ax. Long sections measure the living and the dead: stature, head form, and skulls from the Yukon, for Indians and Eskimo alike. Reports on Kodiak Island, the Alaska Peninsula, and Bristol Bay round out the survey of the western Eskimo region.
52972-letters-from-muskoka:
An emigrant lady wrote these letters from the bush of Muskoka, and Bentley published them at London in 1878. She writes to her child, left behind, and passes over the anguish of the parting. The family sailed from the Thames, a day too early, while carpenters hammered at damage from the last voyage. Her son, their purse scant, took a steerage passage so that his mother and sister could have the first-cabin berths.

Their dog Nero came aboard as a stowaway in a quartermaster's charge. A gale in the Atlantic frightened her worse than any storm off Ireland. The contents promise the year in the bush, letters written two years after, and a wedding in Muskoka. Anecdotes of the Canadian bush thirty years ago and a plea for poor emigrants close the book. The emigrant lady's outlines, as she calls them, are a gentlewoman's Canada: exile priced, and borne.
55980-with-sack-and-stock-in-alaska:
George Broke recounts a climbing venture toward Mount St Elias in a travel book issued in London in 1891. Broke gives the book to the memory of a friend killed on the Dussistock in August 1890. His party sailed from London to Sitka, then worked north toward Yakutat and the great ice fields.

Inside, chapters trace false starts, rain, glacier camps, and attacks of weather on the Chaix Hills and the Libbey and Tyndall glaciers. Broke tells of bears, a blue bear among them, ptarmigan shot for the pot, and a retreat alone with two men. Life at Yakutat, a potlatch, and a canoe run back to Sitka close the tale. Readers get a brisk, hard record of early Alaska mountaineering with sack and rifle.
56303-agate-fossil-beds-national-monumen:
Agate Fossil Beds National Monument, Nebraska, is handbook 107 in a national park series. The Division of Publications at Harpers Ferry Center made it for the Park Service. The park department at Washington stands behind the whole line of handbooks. They are compact guides to the great natural and historic places of the parks. Each is meant to serve before, during, and after a visit, the front pages say.

The book asks what life in North America was like twenty million years ago. Agate gives a glimpse of that time, long before the coming of man. Strange, extinct creatures then roamed the land we know as Nebraska. Part one presents the park, and part two brings the fossil finds to life. Geology and the living land get their study there as well. Part three gives plain guide and reference facts for the road.
60055-the-boy-fortune-hunters-in-alaska:
Floyd Akers sends boys north in The Boy Fortune Hunters in Alaska, printed at Chicago with copyright in 1908. The Reilly and Britton Company made the book. Two more books in the line take the same boys to Panama and Egypt, the front pages say.

A front plate shows the boys captured by the gold hunters. The heads open with bad news, then a found relative, then better fortunes. The boys ship aboard the Flipper for the land of gold. Strange names, Nux and Bryonia, mark one head. Young readers get a brisk tale of ships, ice, and the hunt for wealth in the far north.
62018-the-journal-of-jacob-fowler-narrat:
Jacob Fowler kept this journal of a trapping and trading trip through the far West in 1821 and 1822. Elliott Coues edited it with notes, and Francis Harper of New York published it in 1898 in the American Explorers Series. A copy of a page of Fowler's own hand, with his only known signature, faces the title.

The title maps the route: from Arkansas through the Indian Territory, Oklahoma, Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico, to the sources of the Rio Grande. Fowler's spelling was wild, and the printed text keeps it as he wrote it, with a few clear printer's errors fixed. The manuscript belonged to a Kentucky historian, who lends his voice to the introduction. Coues, a noted naturalist, vouches for the man and the book. Western history readers get a trapper's own day book from the first years of the Santa Fe country.
63553-an-expedition-to-mount-st-elias-al:
Israel C Russell wrote this report of an expedition to Mount St Elias in Alaska, printed in the National Geographic Magazine, volume three, on May 29, 1891. It sold at a dollar fifty. The National Geographic Society of Washington published it. The paper was accepted on March 18, 1891. An introduction treats the southern coast of Alaska.

Part one sums up all earlier probing of the region: Bering in 1741, Cook in 1778, La Pérouse, Dixon, Vancouver, and Belcher. The Coast and Geodetic Survey and the New York Times expedition of 1886 follow. The party's own road runs by canoe in Disenchantment Bay, from Yakutat Bay to Blossom Island. Then it crosses Pinnacle Pass to a first full view of St Elias, with life above the snow line.
66906-ma-rbacka:
Selma Lagerlof wrote Marbacka, her childhood memoir, in Swedish. Howard translated it for Doubleday at New York in 1925. The Stromstad journey opens the contents of the book. The Nursemaid is its first chapter, and Grand Company its second. A drive follows in the early heads of the memoir.

Once a nursemaid at Marbacka was called Back-Kaisa. She must have been all of six feet high, the text remembers. She had a large-featured face, in the child's seeing. Lagerlof's other books stand listed in the front pages. Jerusalem, the Nils books, and the Gosta Berling story stand there. Christ Legends and the Girl from the Marsh Croft join them. The memoir gives the great storyteller her own first world. Servants, parents, and journeys make its small Sweden vivid. Howard's English keeps the child's eye steady throughout.
68707-storm-cloud-on-deka:
Storm Cloud on Deka is a science fiction story by Edward Smith, first printed in Astonishing Stories in June nineteen forty two. It opens inside Tellurian Pharmaceuticals, called the oldest and most careful drug house in civilization. Its board, by unwritten law, holds only men over seventy years old. Rather than make a mistake, do nothing, is the firm's strict creed.

That creed shapes all the firm's dealings across the planets of its trade. It set up branches on other worlds only after a century of trials. It owns no spaceships and sells no goods but its own fine drugs. A consultant in radiation arrives at head office with a report. A branch manager named Graves has come in from the planet Deka. A test is set that will take hours to reach its peak.
70213-yashka:
Yashka is the life of Maria Botchkareva, set down by Isaac Don Levine and first published in 1919. Its full title runs: my life as peasant, exile and soldier. Botchkareva commanded the Russian Women’s Battalion of Death. Constable of London issued the English edition that year.

Her childhood of toil opens the contents of the book. Marriage at fifteen and a little happiness follow in the early chapters. The road to exile and escape from exile fill the next sections. She enlists by the grace of the Tsar, in the chapter so named. First sight of no man’s land, wounds, and eight hours in German hands come next. The revolution at the front and her battalion of women close the arc.
71176-ruth-fielding-in-alaska:
Ruth Fielding in Alaska is a girls' adventure novel by Alice Emerson. Cupples and Leon published it in New York in 1926. Its subtitle names the girl miners of Snow Mountain. The volume stands late in a long series. Twenty-two earlier Ruth Fielding titles are listed in front. A Betty Gordon series by the same hand follows.

Twenty-five chapters pace the northern adventure. A threat opens the tale. A spy and an old enemy complicate it. A man goes overboard midway. Ruth goes to the rescue near the end. The reckoning closes the book. The first scene finds Ruth frowning over a letter. Her friend Helen teases her on the grass. A frozen scowl would mar her beauty forever, Helen warns.
8897-nina-balatka:
Anthony Trollope writes Nina Balatka, a maiden of Prague, born of Christian parents and herself a Christian, who loved a Jew, and this is her story. Nina is the daughter of Josef Balatka, an old Prague merchant, whose wife is dead, and Josef in business has become closely connected with a certain Jewish family. From that connection grows a love across religious lines, in a city where such a match threatens family, business, and standing.

Trollope, writing under a pseudonym at first, treats the romance with his usual attention to money, family pressure, and social judgment. Nina's choice tests loyalty to father, faith, and lover, and the novel's interest lies less in melodrama than in the slow working of prejudice and affection. Readers of Trollope will find a shorter, more exotic novel than the Barsetshire books, but with the same humane eye for how people actually decide.
britannica-1911-abba-arika: 'Abba 'Arika is the headword of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry names a Babylonian amora of the third century, commonly known as Rab. At Sura he set the study of rabbinic traditions on a firm system, the entry states. The Mishnah served as his text. That work led in time to the gathering of the Talmud, the entry holds. Name, place, and one great founding act fill the whole notice, which links the teacher to the long making of rabbinic law.
britannica-1911-akka:
Akka is the name for a group of short folk of the Congo woods, first seen by a white guest in eighteen seventy. Their home is the deep woods of the Aruwimi tract. Each band has its own chief. The entry treats them as the best type of the small folk told of by Herodotus.

Two youths were sent to Italy, and their heights are given in feet. The text notes big round heads, long arms, and short legs that curve in. It also notes that a swelled belly fades with good food, so it is no true mark of the race. They hunt big game with traps and darts.
britannica-1911-balalaika:
Balalaika is a Russian stringed instrument. Peasants prize it across Russia. Ukraine loves it especially there. Its form is said to be primitive. That form has stayed unchanged for ages. A triangular soundboard forms its body.

A vaulted back glues onto that board. The base lets it stand upright alone. A fretted neck rises from the body. Two, three, or four strings stretch along it. Together they usually sound a minor chord. Fingers generally pluck the strings directly. Light sweeping gives charming glissando effects. One string sounds after another that way. Slav races share the instrument widely. Folk songs and dances use its accompaniment. Gipsies play it at rural fairs.
britannica-1911-banjaluka:
Banjaluka is the capital of a district of the same name in Bosnia, on the river Vrbas. Its population in 1895 was 13,666, about half of them Moslems. A military railway ends there, meeting the Hungarian state line at Jasenovac, thirty miles to the north-west. The town holds Catholic and Orthodox bishops, a district court, and an Austrian garrison.

Banjaluka sits at the head of a narrow defile, with steep hills east and west and the Save valley opening north. The citadel and barracks stand where the Crkvina stream joins the Vrbas, near the Ferhadiya Jamia, largest of more than forty mosques. The 1911 Britannica entry also notes ruined Roman baths, one great domed building of the 6th century still in use, fed by the hot springs.
britannica-1911-banka:
Banka, an island of the Dutch East Indies off the east coast of Sumatra, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. A strait near nine miles wide splits it from Sumatra. The island runs 138 miles long and 62 miles wide at most. Its soil is dry and stony, and woods cover most of the land.

The piece gives its stone types, chiefly granite and old slate beds. There are no volcanoes on the island. Banka is famed most for tin, found there in 1710 and held as a state monopoly. The tin lies in veins and in streams, and Chinese crews work it in large groups. Near 120 mines once made up to 12,000 tons a year.
britannica-1911-berka:
Berka is a town and watering-place of Germany, in the grand-duchy of Saxe-Weimar, on the Ilm river and the Weimar-Kranichfeld railway. It stands eight miles south of Weimar and holds some 2,300 people. Its sulphur baths draw crowds of visitors in the summer months.

Berka was once famed for its Cistercian nunnery, a house of white-robed nuns founded in 1251, though the entry gives no word of its later fate. Two miles down the Ilm stands the castle of Burgfarth, a curious stronghold cut partly out of the solid rock itself. The whole notice is short: baths, nunnery and a rock-hewn castle are all it offers the reader.
britannica-1911-britzska:
Britzska, also spelt Britska, comes from the Polish bryczka, a small form of bryka, a goods wagon. It names a kind of carriage that England copied from Austria early in the 19th century. The short entry fixes the word's root, the carriage's home ground and its build in a few lines.

In Poland and Russia, where the type belonged, the britzska ran on four wheels. Its body was long and made of wicker-work, built so a traveller could recline at length on long roads. A calash top, a folding hood, sheltered the riders above. Those three marks, four wheels, wicker body made for reclining and hooded top, define the carriage the notice describes.
britannica-1911-fukuoka:
Fukuoka is a town on the north-west coast of Kiushiu, Japan, in the province of Chikuzen, 90 miles north-north-east of Nagasaki by rail. With Hakata, across a small coast stream, it forms a large centre of population of about 72,000 people. Export trade is growing, and silk weaving leads the local industries, Hakata being noted for its durable silk fabrics.

Fukuoka was once the seat of the powerful daimio of Chikuzen and played a large part in the medieval history of Japan. The renowned temple of Yeiyas in the district was burned during the revolution of 1868. The entry also warns that other Japanese towns share the name. The most important of them is the Fukuoka in Mutsu province in North Nippon, a station on the main line from Tokyo toward Aimori Ura Bay, with about 5000 people.
britannica-1911-iuka:
Iuka, a town in Mississippi, gets a short place entry in the 1911 Britannica. It is the county seat of Tishomingo county, in the north-east corner of the state. The town sits about 25 miles south-east of Corinth and eight miles south of the Tennessee river. Its count rose from 882 in 1900 to 1,221 in 1910. The Southern railway serves it.

Iuka trades in cotton and farm goods, and its mineral springs make it a health resort. Most of the entry goes to one Civil War week. A Confederate force under General Price took the town on the 14th of September 1862. On the 19th a sharp fight with a Federal column under Rosecrans cost some 700 Confederate and 790 Union men. With Grant's force near, Price pulled out the next morning.
britannica-1911-kamchatka:
Kamchatka is a peninsula of northeast Siberia. It runs southwest from the land of the Chukchis for 750 miles, with a width of 80 to 300 miles, between the Sea of Okhotsk and Bering Sea. It forms part of the Russian Maritime Province and covers 104,260 square miles. A flat tundra isthmus joins it to the mainland, sloping gently both ways.

A central mountain chain runs its length, broken under 57 degrees north by a deep gap that matches the valley of the Tighil. Signs in the drainage and in the strike of the rocks point to two chains running parallel to the volcanic chain of the southeast. Glaciers were not known there until 1899, when they were found on the Byelaya and Ushkinskaya mountains, the last 15,400 feet high. Thick Tertiary beds cover the middle west coast, and granites form the south of the central range.
britannica-1911-makalaka: Makalaka is a name used by the Bechuana, Matabele, and kindred peoples for tribes they had conquered or enslaved, says a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Many tribes subdued by the Makololo chief Sebituane around 1830 were called by this name, as David Livingstone recorded. Early writers also used it for some people of Barotseland. More often it pointed to the Makalanga, a tribe classed among the Mashonas, who were brought under Matabele rule.
britannica-1911-makaraka:
The Makaraka, also called Iddio, are a people of Central Africa. They are close kin to the strong Azandeh, or Niam-Niam, race. They hold the Bahr-el-Ghazal west of Lado. They came in the first place from the land of the Kibas, north of the Welle river. Dr W. Junker set them down as among the most trustworthy, hard-working, and keen folk of that region.

The Makaraka are of a reddish-black hue. Their noses are less flat and their cheek-bones less sharp than those of their neighbours, as the article describes them. They do not pull out the front teeth, as many of their neighbours do. Their long, silky hair is built up into the most fanciful shapes with the help of plant stuffs. They are well known for their strength and for their power to endure.
britannica-1911-marie-leszczynska:
Marie Leszczynska, queen consort of France who lived from 1703 to 1768, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. She was born at Breslau on June 23, 1703. Her father, Stanislas, became king of Poland in 1704. As a child in flight she was once lost and found in a stable.

She wed Louis the Fifteenth at Fontainebleau on September 5, 1725. The match was widely seen as beneath the French king. Her one bid in state affairs helped end her husband's favor. Louis then took a string of mistresses, ending with Madame de Pompadour. Marie drew close to her father in Lorraine and died at Versailles in 1768.
britannica-1911-mishawaka:
Mishawaka is a city in Saint Joseph county, Indiana, on the Saint Joseph river. The 1911 Britannica article puts it about eighty miles east of Chicago. Its count more than doubled in ten years, from 5,560 in 1900 to 11,886 in 1910. Two rail lines and electric interurban cars serve the town. It trades in grain and other farm goods from the land around it.

Two dams on the river give much of the power for its factories. The town grew from two plats laid out in the 1830s on each bank. Saint Joseph Iron Works stood on the south side from 1833. Indiana City was laid out on the north side in 1836. In 1839 the two joined as one town under the name Mishawaka. The name came from an Indian village that once stood on part of the site.
britannica-1911-osaka:
Osaka, a city of Japan in the province of Settsu, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It held more than a million people in 1908. It lies in a plain that opens west on Osaka Bay, set on both sides of its river. So many streams and canals cut it that the entry likens it to a Dutch town.

Steamers ran between Osaka and Kobe, and the city was a hub of rail lines. The rail link of 1873 drew much foreign trade to Kobe, so a port for ocean ships was built at Osaka. Most houses were of wood, and a fire in July 1909 burned some twelve thousand of them. Chief sights named are the main street and its iron bridge, the foreign quarter, and many shrines. The castle, mint and arsenal stand out among its public works.
britannica-1911-tanganyika:
Tanganyika is a vast lake in east central Africa, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. The name is said to mean a mixing place, on the word of the explorer Cameron. It is the longest fresh water lake in the world, at just over 400 miles. Its breadth runs from 30 to 45 miles, and its area is about 12,700 square miles. It lies about 2,600 feet above the sea.

The lake fills the south end of the great central rift valley of Africa. That valley stops short at its south point, with Lakes Nyasa and Rukwa beyond a plateau of old rock. To the north, old volcanic ridges dam back Lake Kivu above it. The outlet of Kivu, the Rusizi, has cut through those ridges and now flows into Tanganyika.
britannica-1911-topeka:
Topeka, a city in Kansas, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of the state and the seat of Shawnee county. It stands on both sides of the Kansas river, about sixty miles west of Kansas City. Its people numbered 33,608 in 1900 and 43,684 by the census of 1910. Four rail lines served the city.

The article describes a town laid out in straight order on a level bench of prairie above the river. Among its chief buildings it names the state Capitol, built across near forty years at a cost of more than three million dollars. It calls that building one of the best state houses in the country. A public library, a large hall, a memorial building full of state relics, and a cathedral also stand out in the list.
britannica-1911-york-nebraska:
York, a city in Nebraska, is described in a short gazetteer article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the county seat of York county and lies about forty-six miles west of Lincoln. Its people numbered 5,132 in 1900 and 6,235 in 1910. Two rail lines serve the city, the Burlington road and the North-Western road.

York is the seat of the School of the Holy Family and of York College, founded in 1890 and open to men and women alike. The city sits in a farming and stock raising region. Its works turn out foundry goods, bricks, and flour. York was first settled in 1864 and laid out in 1869. It became a town in 1875 and a chartered city in 1877.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alaska:
Definite knowledge of Alaska came in 1741 through Vitus Bering, a Dane in Russian service, who sailed from Okhoysk to 58 degrees 30 minutes north. Soon Siberian fur hunters coasted the mainland and Aleutian Islands seeking valuable sea otter. Andreian Tolstykh returned to Russia in 1762 after three years there, and his account of Alaska's commercial importance moved Catherine II to send an expedition fostering trade and colonization.

Rival companies disputed the territory. In 1780 traders Grigor Shilikof and Ivan Golikof, leaning on home influence, chiefly Rezanof's, formed the Russian-American Fur Company, which ruled Muscovite Alaska until its 1867 sale to the United States. Gerassim Pribilof discovered in 1786 the Bering Sea seal rookeries, reopening trade with China. Alexander Baranof became the company's general manager in 1790 and presided over a quarter century. The entry then covers Alaska's peoples, missions, schools, orphanages, and hospitals, with 288 children in Catholic institutions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-banjaluka:
Banjaluka is a diocese in western Bosnia, a region of great beauty, on the site of Roman Ad Ladios. By the bull of 5 July 1881, Leo XIII restored Bosnia's Catholic hierarchy with one archdiocese and three dioceses. Banjaluka ranked first among the three, holding four deaneries, thirty-two parishes, and over 80,000 faithful.

Marian Markovic, its first bishop, was consecrated 4 May 1884 as Apostolic administrator only. His first cathedral was a crumbling shed, later replaced by a small church near his residence. Most parishes were then held by Franciscans, and Trappists from Mariastern, founded 1869, had planted three colonies. Sisters of Charity and of the Precious Blood ran hospitals and schools, and in 1900 an Orthodox diocese also centered at Banjaluka.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-ost:
An entry on Christian ostraka, inscriptions on clay, wood, metal, and more hard materials, valued like papyri as literary sources for early Christianity. They come chiefly from the East, above all Egypt, and the greatest number are potsherds inscribed in colour or ink. The oldest Christian ostraka, Greek, date from the fifth century, followed by Coptic and Arabic pieces. Undeciphered Nubian texts survive from the old Christian kingdoms near Aloa on the Blue Nile.

Potsherds served for letters, since the recipient could answer on the back, and for business as bills and receipts. Kaufmann and Falls found the oldest Greek Christian potsherds at Menas in the Libyan desert, deciphered by Bell and Kenyon. They record vine culture, vouchers for money and provisions, help for invalid workmen, and harvest seasons. Coptic ostraka on clergy and monasteries in the Nile valley are especially full.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lincoln-nebra:
Lincoln, in Nebraska, is a diocese suffragan of Dubuque, erected on 2 August 1887 to include the part of Nebraska south of the Platte River. About 17,000 Catholics lived in the section, organized in 27 parishes served by 28 secular and 3 regular priests.

Thomas Bonacum, rector of the Holy Name Church, St. Louis, was named the first bishop, consecrated on 30 November 1887, and took possession on 21 December following. Born near Thurles, Ireland, on 29 January 1847, he emigrated in infancy to St. Louis. He studied at Cape Girardeau's St. Vincent's College and at Würzburg, then was ordained priest at St. Louis on 18 June 1870. As Archbishop Kendrick's theologian he was present at the Third Plenary Council of Baltimore, and was named first Bishop of the proposed Belleville diocese. Propaganda deferred action, and meanwhile Bonacum was named Bishop of Lincoln by Apostolic letters dated 9 August 1887. Statistics for 1910 list 77 priests, 64 churches with resident priests, and 72 missions with churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorenz-leopol:
Lorenz Leopold Haschka was the Viennese poet who wrote Austria's national anthem, born in 1749 and dead in 1827. A Jesuit in youth, he turned to poetry for a living after the order was suppressed in 1773, helped by his pupil Alxinger and by the poetess Karoline Pichler.

Under Josephinist sway he strayed for a time, joined the freemasons, and penned bitter verses against the papacy and the orders. After Joseph II died he returned to Catholic feeling, and his anthem was first sung on 12 February 1797 for Emperor Francis's birthday. He later served in Vienna's university library and taught aesthetics at the Theresianum until 1824.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nebraska:
Nebraska, meaning in English shallow water, holds a central place among the states of the Union and formed part of the Louisiana territory bought from France in 1803. It borders South Dakota in the north, the Missouri River and Iowa in the east, Kansas and Colorado in the south, and Colorado and Wyoming in the west. It spans 76,840 square miles, mostly undulating plain rising gradually from southeast to northwest by about 2,300 feet.

Its chief stream is the Platte, formed by two forks rising in the Rockies and flowing east through the state's centre to the Missouri, with many tributaries. The Niobrara flows north to the Missouri, and the Republican south to the Kansas River. Except in certain seasons, all these rivers run shallow. The 1910 census counted 1,192,214 people. The climate is exceptionally fine, dry and exhilarating, with a mean temperature near 48 degrees. The entry follows the state's settlement, church, parishes and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oecumenius-bi:
Oecumenius, bishop of Trikka in Thessaly around 990, lends a contested name to Greek commentaries on the New Testament. A tenth- or eleventh-century old copy credits him with notes on Revelation that rework Andrew of Caesarea, and later manuscripts attach Acts and epistle commentaries to him.

Those Acts and Catholic epistle notes match Theophylact of Achrida, yet their old copies predate him, suggesting Oecumenius copied Andrew and Theophylact copied Oecumenius. Since the works quote Oecumenius himself, who wrote them stays doubtful in every case. Bardenhewer in 1905 remained doubtful in every case about who wrote these works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-osaka:
Osaka, one of Japan's three municipal prefectures, stands on both banks of the Yodo River along the eastern shore of Osaka Bay. Second city of Japan in people, it led all others in wealth, trade, and industry. Its name, taken to mean great river and cliff, dates only from about 1492. It replaced the older poetic name Naniwa.

Early emperors kept court there, and in the sixteenth century it grew strong as a Buddhist centre. It held out under Nobunaga's persecution until the faithful yielded the town in 1580. Hideyoshi then made it his capital and raised its castle. Modern trade, rail links, and a great harbour scheme pushed its growth further. The entry also covers the Catholic mission, raised to a diocese in 1888, with its churches, schools, and clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-stanislas-:
Stanislas Kostka, a young Polish Jesuit, died at Rome at seventeen after fleeing home to join the Society. Born at Rostkovo near Przasnysz about 28 October 1550, he was second of seven children of Senator John Kostka and Margaret Kryska. His elder brother Paul later attended his beatification in 1605.

Taught at home with severe discipline, the brothers were sent in July 1564 to the Jesuit college at Vienna. Stanislas stood out for amiability, cheerfulness, and religious fervour. Opposed by his father and harshly treated by Paul, he walked to Rome and entered the Society on 28 October 1567. He is said to have foreseen his death days ahead, during the night of 14 to 15 August 1568.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valerian-kali:
Valerian Kalinka was a Polish historian born near Cracow in 1826, who died at Jaroslaw in 1886. He fled Poland in 1846 over political entanglements, worked on the Czas newspaper in 1848, and finally took refuge in Paris. There he wrote his first work, Galicia und Cracovie, a historical and social picture of the country from 1772 to 1850.

He then planned a history of the Polish emigration but chose instead to edit a weekly called Political Polish News, whose chief writers were himself and Klaczko. Though banned everywhere but Posen, it ran four years and covered every side of Polish national life. His articles show a practical grasp of law, administration, history, and statistics, mostly on Poland's inner life. The entry follows his later historical work.
doe-osti-3007680-synthesis-and-crystal-s:
Synthesis routes and crystal structures for alkali iron phosphate crystals are given by Saehwa Chong, Brian Riley, Mark Bowden, Joshua Silverstein, and Nate Brown in a December 2025 Pacific Northwest lab report. The alkalis covered are sodium, rubidium, and caesium.

The team paired X-ray diffraction with scanning electron microscopy, energy dispersive spectroscopy, and optical microscopy to solve the structures. Full results are saved as crystallographic information files, the standard format other researchers can reuse. Much of the volume is dense tables of diffraction intensities and atomic positions. This crystal family draws interest for phosphate waste forms, where iron phosphates can lock up problem elements.
for-greater-things-the-story-of-saint-st:
William T. Kane, a Jesuit priest, told the life of Saint Stanislaus Kostka in For Greater Things as a story for the young. Stanislaus, a Polish nobleman's son schooled in Vienna, resolves to enter the Jesuits against his family's will. In August 1567, not yet seventeen, he walks out of Vienna in splendid clothes with a peasant's bundle, bound on foot for Augsburg and then Rome, four hundred miles and more.

His brother pursues him; illness nearly kills him; the noviceship in Rome receives him at last. Kane follows the contents from early days through the runaway journey to the aftermath of an early death. The title echoes the Jesuit motto of doing all for the greater glory of God.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KDKA_KDKA: A sheet of Westinghouse Broadcasting Company letterhead dated November 24, 1975 lists the stations of the KDKA group. No letter text is present; the sheet survives as printed stationery alone. Corporate letterhead is pure ephemera, meant to be written on and thrown away, and this example documents the broadcasting group's station lineup as the company printed it in 1975.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SchevchenkoArka:
Tad Szulc wrote this article about the defection of Arkady N. Shevchenko. Shevchenko was the United Nations Under-Secretary-General for political and Security Council affairs. He was, Szulc writes, potentially the richest diplomatic prize of the SALT II talks. The article asks whether Moscow had suspected he had ties to a former FBI deep plant.

Shevchenko was the highest-ranking Soviet official ever to defect, and he had spied for the United States while in place. His story joined diplomacy and espionage in one career. Szulc, a veteran foreign correspondent, weighs what Moscow knew and when. The article preserves the defection as Washington argued about it: a triumph with a worm of doubt inside, reported while SALT II hung on the outcome.
muir-travels-alaska:
Travels in Alaska, published in 1915, the year after John Muir's death, gathers his journals from trips in 1879, 1880, and 1890. Muir explored Alaska's coast by canoe and steamship with missionary companions. Glaciers drew him north again and again.

He describes the great ice rivers of Glacier Bay and the Tlingit people who guided him. The story of Stickeen, the brave little dog on the glacier, became his most loved tale. Storms, crevasses, and northern lights fill the rest. The book completes Muir's Alaska work and shows his wonder undimmed by age. Muir's editors shaped the journals into chapters after his death.
nina-balatka:
Anthony Trollope opens Nina Balatka with its whole conflict in a few lines. Nina is a maiden of Prague, born of Christian parents and herself a Christian. Yet she loves a Jew, and this, the narrator says, is her story. Her mother is dead when the tale begins.

Her father Josef, an old Prague merchant, did business with Trendellsohn, a Jew of the Jews' quarter. Jews then had to live in that one allotted part of town. Trendellsohn's son Anton is the man Nina loves. Josef had lately left a rich Christian partner, Karil Zamenoy, for this new tie. Love across a hard line drives the novel.
podcast-dannyjones-Flz50uERwKA:
Jeffrey Mishlove is a parapsychologist who holds one of the few doctorates in his field and won a famous essay contest on evidence for life after death. With Danny Jones, he discusses the military's psychic spies, his years of contact with Scientology, and the cases he believes best prove survival of consciousness.

Mishlove's manner is calm and scholarly, a contrast with the show's more fevered guests. He reviews the remote viewing record, the mediums he has tested, and the standards he applies. Skeptics remain unconvinced by his field, and he knows their arguments well enough to state them himself. The episode is a measured tour of parapsychology by its most credible living representative. Listeners can judge whether his evidence carries the weight he gently claims for it.
